query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, moderate additions of Al promote a controlled degree of atomic ordering (e.g., formation of a B2‐like precipitate phase within a disordered matrix) that stabilizes the overall phase by counterbalancing the high configurational entropy of the disordered state. This ordering mediates a balance between strengthening (through precipitate hardening and defect pinning) and retention of high ductility/toughness across temperature extremes (from cryogenic to high temperature) as well as improved environmental and radiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic or near-equiatomic disordered single-phase FCC or BCC solid-solution alloy with low Al content (minimal atomic ordering).
generation.intervention: Systematically increase the Al content while keeping Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni ratios constant to reach a threshold where ordered nano-precipitates (e.g., B2 phase) emerge.
generation.conditions: Samples to be processed under identical homogenization and cooling conditions to ensure that the only variable is the Al concentration; tests performed at elevated temperatures, under radiation exposure simulations, and at cryogenic temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Induced nano-scale ordered precipitates (e.g., B2-type phase) embedded in the disordered solid solution.
generation.mechanism: Al additions increase the ordering enthalpy relative to the configurational entropy, triggering local atomic ordering. The ordered precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion (enhancing high-temperature strength) and serve as stable sites for defect annihilation under radiation, while also contributing to microstructural features that promote toughness at cryogenic temperatures. This dual role helps retain a balanced combination of mechanical strength, environmental resistance, and radiation tolerance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline low-Al alloy, alloys with moderate Al additions will show the emergence of a secondary ordered phase, which will correlate with increased yield strength at elevated temperatures, improved radiation defect resistance, and maintained or enhanced cryogenic toughness. These alloys should display microstructural evidence (by XRD/TEM) of ordered precipitates and exhibit a tailored balance between hardness and ductility.
generation.baseline: Low or minimal Al content alloys that remain in a disordered single-phase state without significant precipitate formation, exhibiting lower yield strength at high temperature and less radiation tolerance despite potentially high cryogenic toughness.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies within a controlled window of Al content where the induced ordering is sufficient to produce strengthening precipitates but not so high as to trigger detrimental phase segregation or embrittlement. It is confined to the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni system under near-equiatomic conditions and standard processing routes.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative role of atomic ordering is supported, the precise Al concentration required and the quantitative improvements in properties (e.g., magnitude of strength increase or radiation tolerance) are uncertain. It is also unclear how competing kinetic effects during cooling may affect the extent of ordering.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy samples with systematically varied Al content across the critical range. Process all samples identically to avoid processing-induced microstructural differences. Characterize each sample using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to quantify the presence and volume fraction of any ordered (B2-like) phases. Perform mechanical testing at high temperatures, under simulated radiation conditions (e.g., ion irradiation), and at cryogenic temperatures to assess strength, radiation tolerance, and toughness.
measurements: Phase identification (XRD/TEM) to detect and quantify ordered precipitate formation.
High-temperature mechanical tests (yield strength, creep behavior).
Radiation tolerance tests (post-irradiation defect density via microscopy or positron annihilation spectroscopy).
Cryogenic toughness measurements (e.g., SENB fracture toughness tests).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing Al content does not lead to the formation of an ordered secondary phase or the appearance (and magnitude) of such ordering does not correlate with the expected improvements in high-temperature strength, radiation resistance, and cryogenic toughness relative to the low-Al baseline, then the hypothesis that atomic ordering governs phase stability and the resultant balanced properties would be falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are solid solutions consisting of five or more metallic elements in approximately equimolar ratios with elemental compositions typically between 5–35 atomic percent (at.%). They have attracted increasing attention, especially as structural materials, due to their remarkable mechanical strength and resistance to oxidation and fatigue at ambient and elevated temperatures. The compositional complexity does not automatically imply microstructural complexity due to the high mixing entropy. Often, an operational definition for HEAs is a solid-solution phase stabilized by the higher configurational entropy that increases with increasing temperature. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), which were originally developed as concentrated solid solutions of multiple principal elements in equal, or near equal, atomic ratios, have drawn progressively increasing attention over the past decade. Unlike single principal-element alloys, their complex alloy compositions and elemental distribution, together with crystal lattice distortion induced by atomic-size mismatch (depending upon relative atomic sizes), can have a significant effect on the activity of their crystal defects and hence mechanical properties. Although HEAs were initially designed to benefit from single-phase stabilization,, single-phase HEAs are actually not that common, and of those that do exist, only a few display excellent damage-tolerance in the form of combinations of high strength, ductility, and toughness. The well-studied equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi Cantor alloy and its derivatives, in particular the CrCoNi alloy, show exceptional damage-tolerance which progressively improves at cryogenic temperatures, although even these alloys do not have yield (as opposed to ultimate tensile) strengths that are comparable to some advanced steels.
